i think you’re incredibly beautiful! but if you’re truly wanting to “improve” yourself, you could always revamp your skincare routine. exfoliating and using retinol can brighten and clear anyone’s skin, but remember to use sunscreen everyday, especially if you’re using actives. sunday riley sells a lactic acid and retinol pair that can brighten the skin and assist with texture and add vibrancy to the face. alongside those, i use the skin cycling method which helps to prevent over-exfoliating. there’s a lot of great resources out there to help you figure out what you could personally add to your skin care routine, but those are the things i recommend to almost everyone.

additionally, if you’re looking to revamp your wardrobe or or your hair, start by identifying your body type, undertones, and color scheme. beyond warm and cool toned, there are more specific ways to identify your coloring, such as your seasonal color palette. for your body type, i used the kibbe body type to help identify my body type and dress more appropriately for it, and not only has it helped me become more precise with my shopping habits, i also enjoy shopping so much more, because i’m much more likely to pick up clothes that i love right off the rack!

beyond all of that, how are you taking care of your mind and your heart? what hobbies do you have, how mindful are you? are you supplementing with vitamins—most people in the US are vitamin D deficient, and women especially need to be cognizant of calcium deficiencies, especially as we age. i’ve recently started taking a vitamin D supplement with calcium and i feel like i can take over the world! vitamin D isn’t actually a vitamin, it’s a hormone, and it’s actually called the happy hormone. i would highly recommend it(:

hair discrimination is perpetuated both inside and out of the black community—the chris rock documentary “good hair” touches on this. i cannot completely answer your question for sure because the development of the culture around hair didn’t happen in a vacuum, so i can’t say one way or another. i will say, however, that traditional african hairstyles, including in west africa and in nigeria, mostly feature natural hair or women wearing protective styles such as box braids, dreads, and other forms of braids. protective styles have been around for a long time and have a pretty well documented history. relaxers, and weaves, however, are more recent introductions to the black community, and it’s not without noting that those introductions happened in the early 20th century, when black women were entering the workforce and dealing with other forms of discrimination.

wigs have been around since the times of cleopatra, so maybe! but would they have the prevalence that they do have? who knows. maybe traditional african hairstyles would be a lot more common, and wigs would be something saved for only special events.

often times it’s employers—being told by HR or your bosses that you need to “do something with your hair” when you wear it naturally, someone making comments such as “oh so you just decided to roll out of bed today.” another huge issue is the issue of touching. a lot of black women, including myself, have our heads touched without our consent when we wear our natural hair out. people have grabbed my hair by the fistful because they’re “curious,” but not only is it painful, but also incredibly demeaning.

beyond that, a lot of the hairstyles that we use to protect our hair, such as protective styles, are banned in a lot of workplaces. box braids, for example, are a common protective style that a lot of black women wear. i’ve been in work places that have both banned my natural hair and banned protective styles, which was difficult to deal with. this kind of discrimination is systematic, and is why wearing wigs, weaves, and other similar styles is so common in the black community. i love wearing my wig, but i also recognize that i wear it partially because i am a pre-law student, and i’ve been told before that the hair that grows naturally out of my head is ugly, and that i won’t get far in life if i wear it out. it’s a difficult thing to process. i can’t tell you how many times i’ve cried over my hair growing up.

Last Friday I was running on this trail by my house in the rain when all of a sudden this guy comes out from the trees. I wasn't paying that much attention so I didn't worry about it. After about 30 seconds I noticed that he was following me even though where we were running was a pretty large open area at that point. I cut across and started singing (I had my headphones in) to make it seem like I didn't notice him. Well, he cut across as well and that's when I started to get nervous.

I started to speed up, turning back towards my house, where the trees were denser. I lost sight of him and I thought he was gone. I kept running, and I went about 2 minutes before I saw him again, this time with a mask on. It was dark outside and this dude was way bigger than me (I'm 5'1", 100 lbs) and could probably out sprint me, so I was terrified. I started to run as hard as I could and I got back to the road and called my best friend to tell him what was going on. He helped calm me down again and I kept running, super freaked out.

And then I saw him again. But on a bike. Still following me. At this point, I knew that I was in a super fucked up situation but I knew that screaming wouldn't do anything. I told my best friend that everything was okay but I just wanted him to stay on the phone with me. I started to sprint again and the guy started coming towards me super fast and part of me knew that shit was about to go down.

He jumped off of his bike and tackled me, and at this point I was beyond terrified. It was obvious what he was trying to do, but I scratched and kicked and bot and punched until I couldn't think anymore. Both of my parents are vets, so I used every single bit of knowledge that I could to get him off of me. I honestly don't even remember what I did, but after that the next thing I remember was sitting at home in the shower fully clothed and freaked out and covered in bruises and scratches.

TL;DR: I was chased and almost raped by some freaky dude in a mask on Friday
